title: Solve Problems with Unit Rates
objective: I can solve real-world problems by using unit rates to compare options.
model: unit rate as the amount for 1 (divide the bundle into equal groups), compared per item on a double number line or ratio table

widgets.component: unit-rate warm-up (price of one, items in 1 minute, total from the rate)
widgets.root: Divide-then-scale, the lesson's worked example; num items carry wrong-path feedback (inverted division, multiplication, subtraction).

widgets.component: better buy, unit rate, scale by the rate, unit-price tables, 'compared totals' and 'divided in the wrong order' mistakes
widgets.root: Keys recomputed ($0.75 vs $0.80, 3/min, 105 pages, $1.60 vs $1.75, 80 tokens, 540 widgets, table rates). The two err items trap exactly the lesson's misconceptions.

widgets.component: generated rate, find-the-quantity and least-cost problems
widgets.root: Generator stems carry both stores' deals and the amount needed; answers independently checked by the repo test.

widgets.component: mixing station: drag a divider to split a bundle into equal groups, one per item
widgets.root: A manipulable model of 'unit rate = amount for one'; an uneven split gets a miss message that names the total the groups make against the item count, and L4 compares two bundles, including a tie, with a 'compare the cost of ONE item' prompt.

widgets.component: 'What is Printer A's unit rate?', 'Printer B's', 'Which printer is faster, and how long for 600 tickets?'
widgets.root: The stems refer to Printer A and Printer B but no stem, table or viz states their tickets and minutes (the answer explanations use 150 tickets in 5 minutes and 200 in 8). The student cannot answer them; the data sits in connect.check only.
widgets.replacement: Rewrite the three items as one stand-alone scenario: 'Printer A prints 150 tickets in 5 minutes. Printer B prints 200 tickets in 8 minutes.' with a table viz (Printer | Tickets | Minutes). 5.1 key 30 per minute, 5.2 key 25 per minute, 5.3 key 'Printer A, 20 minutes' (600 ÷ 30). Keep the existing distractors (150, 5 and 8 are raw totals or the wrong division order, 24 minutes is B's time) so each wrong choice still names a misconception.

widgets.component: miles per gallon from 195 mi on 6 gal
widgets.root: Self-contained; key 32.5 correct; 1,170 is the trapped multiplication.

widgets.component: generated unit-rate problems up to a two-rate chain (gallons per minute times cents per gallon)
widgets.root: L4 7 gal/min x $0.05 x 4 min = $1.40 verified; answer given in dollars as the stem says.

widgets.component: 'Find the Unit Rate Error': Deal 1 as 5 ÷ $8.75 = 0.57 lb per dollar, Deal 2 as 3 ÷ $5.10 = 0.59, 'so Deal 2 is the better buy'; error key = step 2
widgets.root: Pounds per dollar is a legitimate unit rate and 0.59 > 0.57 correctly picks Deal 2 (the fix text admits 'Deal 2 is still the better buy'). The key marks a correct step as the error, so a student who reasons correctly is told they are wrong. Also the first step's label and work fields are swapped (the question is printed as the step label, 'Compare two deals' as the work).
widgets.replacement: Replace with an error that is wrong: Dmitri divides 5 ÷ $8.75 for Deal 1 but $5.10 ÷ 3 for Deal 2 (mixed rates, 0.57 lb per dollar versus $1.70 per lb), so the tap target is the step that compares them; or keep both lb per dollar and add a final step 'the lower number is the better buy' (wrong, because more pounds per dollar is better). Fix the swapped l/w in step 1 (setup sentence in the setup row).

widgets.component: token deals, drone miles per minute, glue price per ounce, screws savings, printer hours, 'buy 3 get 1 free'
widgets.root: All keys recomputed ($0.12 vs $0.11 and $110; 0.75 vs 0.70; $0.30/$0.26/$0.30 and $16.64; $6 saved; 20 hours; $3.00 versus $3.25). 2.7 is a good unit-rate trap.

widgets.component: mixing station: build two paint mixes with the same amount of the first ingredient, then tap the mix with more of the second
widgets.root: That is the 3-5 'compare ratio relationships' method (make one term match), on colour mixtures with no price or per-unit quantity. The 3-8 objective is to compare options by unit rate, which the lesson's own worked example does by dividing $60 by 500 tokens.
widgets.replacement: Use ratiomix mode=unitrate at L3-L4 with two priced bundles of different sizes (e.g. 6 for $4.50 and 10 for $7.00): the student drags the divider on each bundle until each group is the price of one item, then picks the better buy; include a tie, and a 'items per dollar, higher is better' variant so the lower/higher direction is trapped.

widgets.component: two bundles split into equal groups, pick the better buy (tie possible)
widgets.root: Exactly the lesson's idea in a manipulable form, including the tie.

widgets.component: lower is better / higher is better for six rates
widgets.root: Teaches the direction of 'better' for cost-per-item versus items-per-dollar; cards verified.

widgets.component: detective items, paint per litre, coolant hours, bolts, ratio-table price check, write-your-own
widgets.root: Keys recomputed ($0.72, 16 hours, 80 bolts, $13.00 versus $13.60 per litre, 12 m for $17.00 breaks $1.50 per m). Table viz draws a proportional ratio table.

typography: Challenge §2.1 step 1 stores the setup sentence in the label field and 'Compare two deals' in the work field (display swap)
